comments.body: The guard checks the comment in isolation, but interpolation later runs over the whole SQL, so `SELECT 1 /*k='$__timeFilter(t'*/ WHERE (x = 1)` is preserved and then interpolated across the comment boundary. I tested it locally and got `SELECT 1 /*k='t'*/ WHERE (x = 1 BETWEEN FROM_UNIXTIME(1000) AND FROM_UNIXTIME(2000)`, a corrupted query that contradicts the PR's "can never smuggle a live macro" claim. Same flaw at `grafana-postgresql-datasource/macros.go:133` and `mssql/sqleng/macros.go:112`.

`sqleng.Interpolate` does blind `strings.ReplaceAll` of `$__interval`, `$__interval_ms`, `$__unixEpochFrom()`/`To()` on the raw SQL before the macro engine calls `stripSQLComments`, so `/*i='$__interval'*/` reaches the guard already rewritten to `/*i='2m'*/` and is preserved with an interpolated value. This is inconsistent with stripping paren-form macros, and it makes the "stable" attribution tag change on every zoom.

This drops the remainder (`"SELECT 1 /*ab" becomes `"SELECT 1 "`), but Postgres/MSSQL keep the old fall-through that leaks the final byte back into the query (`"SELECT 1 b"`, and `"SELECT 1 /*ab'"` become `"SELECT 1 '"`). Please either port the fix to all three or note the intentional divergence, as written the parallel implementations silently differ.

The spec escapes single quotes in values as `\'` and URL-encodes keys (which may contain `%`), but `[^']*` and the key charset reject both. I verified `/*controller='it\'s'*/` and `/*a%20b='x'*/` are dropped whole. The feature the PR advertises silently fails for those tags with no signal.

Now that a package-level `macroRegExp` compiled from the same `sExpr` exists, `Interpolate` should use it and drop this per-call compile, otherwise the guard's regex and the actual interpolation regex can drift apart, which would reintroduce exactly the bug the guard prevents. Note that this exists in the implementations for the other SQL variants too.

I had Claude go over this alongside the Codex pass. I agree with all three Codex P1s (device-comm destroy before unregister, stale `devcomm_registry_` on replacement, and `nccl_wait_signal` bypassing the liveness guard), so please treat those as blockers too.

Three additional blockers from that review, quoted below with my framing. The first one is the one I care most about, since the PR's own test codifies the broken recovery path. The second is a straight deletion that shrinks the ROCm blast radius rather than growing it.

> **1. A stale handle is unrecoverable, and the error message points at an action the PR's own test asserts will fail.**
>
> `NCCLSymmetricMemory.cu:874` calls `check_liveness()` on the `symm_mems_` cache hit and throws, but never evicts `symm_mems_[key]` or `allocation->peer_alloc_infos_[group_name]`. The message says "Rendezvous again after initializing the successor process group", yet `test_retained_handle_rejected_across_same_name_restart` asserts that `symm_mem.rendezvous(tensor, old_group_name)` still raises after the successor PG is up and registered. The backing `ncclMemAlloc` block is still valid, so the recoverable behavior is available: on a stale cache hit, evict the cached handle and the stale `pai` and re-register the window against the successor comm. If permanent rejection is the intent, the message needs to say the tensor must be freed and re-allocated, not re-rendezvoused.
>
> **2. The ROCm registry-key divergence is an identity transform, and its one real delta is a name collision.**
>
> `ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:986` does `this->setGroupUid(options_->group_name)` in the constructor, before `eagerConnectSingleDevice()` and before any lazy `initNCCLComm()`. So at every register/unregister site `getGroupUid() == options_->group_name`, and `distributed_c10d.py` sets `options.group_name` to the Python-visible group name. The nccl2 backend already publishes with `getGroupUid()` (`nccl2/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:699`), and this PR's own `backend_name="nccl"` lifecycle test passes on ROCm, which empirically proves that key resolves. The premise in the comment at `ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp:3346` ("which is not what `getGroupUid()` returns") does not hold.
>
> That leaves `symmMemGroupName()` and the three `#ifdef USE_ROCM` branches doing nothing, except for the `"" -> "0"` fallback, which is actively harmful: `Backend::Options::group_name` defaults to empty (`Backend.hpp:114`), so any C++-constructed `ProcessGroupNCCL` (for example `test/cpp/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCLErrorsTest.cpp:52`) now registers under the literal name of the default Python group. Aliasing distinct process groups onto one registry key is exactly what the identity-safe unregister was added to prevent. Suggest dropping the divergence and calling `unregister_comm(getGroupUid(), ncclComm->getNcclComm())` on both platforms.
>
> **3. `nccl_reduce_scatter_offset.cu:339` changes CUDA behavior, which the description says does not happen.**
>
> The `owned_sizes[j] <= uint16 max` `TORCH_CHECK` sits in the shared validation loop, above the `#ifndef USE_ROCM`. It is the right fix, since the previous behavior was silent truncation to `owned_sizes[j] % 65536`, but it turns working-but-wrong CUDA calls into hard errors. That contradicts "CUDA behavior is unchanged" and "Every behavioral delta above is under `USE_ROCM`", and reviewers are relying on those claims to bound the blast radius. Please call it out in the description, or land it separately as the CUDA bug fix it is.

On CI: worth noting that `skipIfRocmVersionLessThan((10, 1))` means trunk, periodic-mi300 and periodic-mi200 all collect 49 items and skip 49, so the only live signal for this feature is `rocm-preview`, which is not merge-blocking. The RCCL version and build-probe gates already cover the real requirements. If the 10.1 floor is load-bearing for a reason beyond those, a comment saying why would help; otherwise dropping it would buy real coverage.

A v1 dashboard passes through `v2alpha1` when it is converted to `v2beta1`. The `v2alpha1` transformation type does not have this new `refId` field, so the value is lost along the way. I confirmed this with a conversion test.

body:
I set up a small throwaway app that announces `discovery: [mcp]` and ran this against it. The flow works nicely, and the entry ends up with the Supervisor uuid as unique ID and the app slug in its data, as intended.

Two things I would like to see addressed before this lands, both in `async_step_hassio` — see the inline comment below and my reply in the existing thread on line 212.

comments.body:
One case I'd like us to handle: `discovery.json` is Supervisor-internal state and isn't part of a backup — backups cover `homeassistant`, `share`, `addons/local`, `ssl` and `media`. So restoring onto a new system gives the app a fresh discovery uuid while the restored config entry still holds the old one. The URL is unchanged, so the flow aborts on the URL match and the entry keeps a uuid that no longer exists anywhere in Supervisor. Uninstalling the app then leaves the entry behind (`async_process_del` matches on `unique_id`), and the entry's `discovery_keys` are stale too, so re-discovery on removal is broken as well.

That's the normal migrate-to-new-hardware path, so I'd rather not leave it. Wyoming handles the equivalent case by re-linking the entry:

```python
for entry in self._iter_entries(uri.hostname, uri.port):
    return self.async_update_reload_and_abort(
        entry,
        unique_id=discovery_info.uuid,
        reload_even_if_entry_is_unchanged=False,
        reason="already_configured",
    )
```

Suggestion, combined with the reordering in the other thread:

```python
await self.async_set_unique_id(discovery_info.uuid)
self._abort_if_unique_id_configured(updates={CONF_URL: url})

# A restore onto a new system gives the app a new discovery uuid while the
# restored entry still holds the old one. Re-link it so that Supervisor can
# still remove the entry together with the app.
for entry in self._async_current_entries(include_ignore=False):
    if entry.source == SOURCE_HASSIO and entry.data.get(CONF_URL) == url:
        return self.async_update_reload_and_abort(
            entry,
            unique_id=discovery_info.uuid,
            reload_even_if_entry_is_unchanged=False,
            reason="already_configured",
        )

self._async_abort_entries_match({CONF_URL: url})
```

Note the `SOURCE_HASSIO` gate, which is where I'd deviate from Wyoming: a manually created entry can't be fully adopted anyway, since `async_update_entry` can't change `source` and `async_process_del` requires it. Re-linking one would leave it half-managed — uuid updated but still not removable — which seems worse than leaving it alone. Gated this way, adoption is all-or-nothing: complete for entries that were already Supervisor-managed, no-op for everything else.

Worth a test: existing entry with the old uuid, discovery arrives with a new uuid and the same URL, assert `already_configured` and that the entry now carries the new uuid.

I do think Supervisor should also keep discovery state in backups — most likely alongside the app metadata so it is restored together with the app, plus pruning of stale messages when an app's config changes. I'll follow up on that separately. But that only helps backups taken after such a fix, so Core should cope regardless.

On the side: `uptime_kuma` and `pyload` use exactly the same uuid-as-unique-id pattern and have the same gap, so whatever we settle on here is probably worth porting to those two later. Not something this PR needs to solve.

body:
Hi @totoroot ,

thank you for this PR!  Glob support for `entityFilename` fills a real gap, especially for monorepo users on CE/free GitLab who cannot rely on `useSearch`.
And finally being able to match both `.yaml` and `.yml` catalog files with a single pattern like `**/catalog-info.y?(a)ml` is such a nice touch. Both of these have been long-standing pain points for the community. (I also feel the pain of having to explain that the extension is y**a**ml , especially when you have .gitlab-ci.yml files everywhere ^.^)

A few things I’d love to see addressed before this moves out of draft:

### `useSearch: true` + glob silently falls back to tree scan

This feels like a potentially breaking behavior change for Premium users. A warning log is pretty easy to miss, and users could unknowingly lose search-based discovery without realizing it.

Personally, I’d lean toward throwing an explicit error that forces users to intentionally set `useSearch: false` when using glob patterns. At minimum, this interaction should be clearly documented in the config schema and docs.

### File deletion via push broken for glob patterns

The `onRepoPush` flow currently gates on `getProjectCatalogFiles()`, which scans the repo tree after the delete has already happened.

By the time the push event is processed, the file is gone. The scan returns `[]`, the early return fires, and the `removed` array from the commit never gets processed. That means the entity stays in the catalog until the next scheduled full refresh.

This is a **pre-existing issue** in exact filename mode as well, so it is not introduced by this PR. However, the new implementation makes it more noticeable. Since the benefits of this PR outweigh this concern and the full scan eventually does remove the entity, I would suggest opening a follow-up issue so it does not get lost.

### Stray `node-fetch` dependency

`node-fetch` was added to `package.json`, but I could not find it used anywhere in the diff. Worth removing before merge.

### Dead parameter in `getFilesMatchingConfig`

`catalogFileMatcher: Minimatch` is only referenced in the log message. The actual filtering goes through `this.filePathMatches()`, which uses `this.catalogFileMatcher` from the instance directly.

The behavior is correct, but the signature implies the caller controls the matching when it actually does not. I think that will be a little confusing for the next person reading the code.

Simplest fix is probably removing the parameter entirely and referencing `this.catalogFileMatcher.pattern` directly in the log line.

### Performance implications worth documenting

This changes the API call pattern from roughly `O(projects)` HEAD checks to `O(projects × files)` recursive tree scans when glob patterns are enabled.

For larger installations, that is a pretty meaningful shift. Would be great to call this out in the docs/config schema so users can make an informed tradeoff before adopting glob patterns.

---

Overall, really nice work. Thanks for thinking about backward compatibility as well as the tests!
